meta.label: Over-the-counter medicine
meta.attribution: Covers medicine-cabinet staples that cut across the whole non-prescription aisle: pain relievers and fever reducers (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin), antihistamines for allergy (cetirizine, levocetirizine, diphenhydramine, loratadine, fexofenadine), and acid reducers for heartburn (famotidine, omeprazole, esomeprazole), each compared brand name against the store-brand version with the same active ingredient and dose. Other decisions in this catalogue go deeper on a single ailment: pain relief; cold, flu and cough remedies; allergy and hay fever treatments; and digestive and stomach remedies, each with room for a fuller roster of its own. Assembled from FDA-approved Drug Facts labels published on DailyMed, the FDA and GAO on the OTC drug monograph system, and Cleveland Clinic, plus Target product pages for prices (Target prices vary by store, so compare per-dose ratios rather than exact dollar figures). Scope is the US market. Not medical advice. The lowest-risk choice depends on age, pregnancy, allergies, and conditions such as liver, kidney, heart, or stomach disease; ask a pharmacist or doctor if unsure. Reviewed 2026-10. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare over-the-counter medicine by body safety, cost, and everyday access.

products.name: Tylenol Extra Strength

economical.note: Target lists Tylenol Extra Strength Caplets, 100 count, at $10.99, which is $0.11 per 500 mg caplet.

health.note: DailyMed's Tylenol Extra Strength label states severe liver damage may occur if you take more than 4,000 mg of acetaminophen in 24 hours, with other acetaminophen-containing products, or with 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day, and caps adult dosing at 6 caplets (3,000 mg) in 24 hours. It carries no stomach, kidney, or cardiovascular warning at labeled doses.

accessibility.note: Tylenol is a nationally marketed brand under the FDA's internal analgesic OTC monograph, not a single retailer's store label, unlike Target's up & up acetaminophen.

products.description: The market-leading acetaminophen brand, priced well above the store-brand version that carries the identical 500 mg dose and the identical FDA liver warning.

products.name: up & up Acetaminophen Extra Strength

economical.note: Target lists up & up Acetaminophen Extra Strength Caplets, 100 count, at $1.99, which is $0.02 per 500 mg caplet, about a fifth of the Tylenol Extra Strength price for the same dose.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's Acetaminophen Extra Strength states severe liver damage may occur if you take more than 4,000 mg of acetaminophen in 24 hours, and caps adult dosing at 6 units (3,000 mg) in 24 hours, the same threshold and wording as the Tylenol label.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists Target Corporation as the label holder for this product, meaning it is Target's own store brand, sold only through Target stores and target.com rather than a nationally licensed brand carried by multiple chains.

products.description: Target's store-brand acetaminophen, the same 500 mg dose and the same FDA-mandated liver warning as Tylenol Extra Strength, at about a fifth of the price.

products.name: Advil

economical.note: Target lists Advil Pain Reliever/Fever Reducer Tablets, 100 count, at $10.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.11 per 200 mg ibuprofen tablet.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Haleon's Advil Tablets (ibuprofen 200 mg, the product priced above) states the product contains an NSAID that may cause severe stomach bleeding, with higher risk over age 60, with a history of stomach ulcers or bleeding, on blood thinners or steroids, with 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day, or taken longer than directed, and that NSAIDs other than aspirin increase the risk of heart attack, heart failure, and stroke, a risk that can appear in the first weeks of use.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists Advil under its own FDA new drug application, held by the manufacturer rather than a retailer, so it is a nationally marketed brand, not a single retailer's private label, unlike Target's up & up ibuprofen.

products.description: The market-leading ibuprofen brand, carrying the FDA's stomach-bleeding and heart attack and stroke warnings required of every NSAID.

products.name: up & up Ibuprofen

economical.note: Target lists up & up Ibuprofen (NSAID) Tablets, 100 count, at $1.99, which is $0.02 per 200 mg tablet, about a fifth of the Advil price for the same dose.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's ibuprofen states this NSAID may cause severe stomach bleeding, with the same risk factors as the Advil label, and that NSAIDs other than aspirin increase the risk of heart attack, heart failure, and stroke, which can be fatal.

accessibility.note: DailyMed's label names Target Corporation as the label holder, meaning this is Target's own store brand, sold only through Target stores and target.com.

products.description: Target's store-brand ibuprofen, the same 200 mg dose and the same NSAID warnings as Advil, at about a fifth of the price.

products.name: Zyrtec 24 Hour Allergy Relief

economical.note: Target lists Zyrtec 24 Hour Allergy Relief Tablets, 30 count, at $19.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.67 per 10 mg cetirizine tablet, tied with Claritin and Allegra for the most expensive dose in this roster.

health.note: DailyMed's Zyrtec label states drowsiness may occur, to avoid alcoholic drinks, and that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness.

accessibility.note: Zyrtec is a nationally marketed brand under the FDA's OTC antihistamine framework, not a single retailer's private label, unlike Target's up & up cetirizine.

products.description: The main cetirizine antihistamine brand; even this newer-generation formula still warns on its own label that drowsiness may occur.

products.name: up & up Cetirizine

economical.note: Target lists up & up Cetirizine Hydrochloride Allergy Relief Tablets, 30 count, at $6.69 (prices vary by store), which is $0.22 per 10 mg tablet, about a third of the Zyrtec price.

health.note: up & up cetirizine is 10 mg cetirizine hydrochloride, the same active ingredient and dose as Zyrtec, and carries the same drowsiness and alcohol warning as the Zyrtec label.

accessibility.note: up & up is Target's own store brand; the product page compares its active ingredient to Zyrtec and it is sold only through Target stores and target.com.

products.description: Target's store-brand cetirizine, the same 10 mg dose and the same drowsiness warning as Zyrtec, at under half the price.

products.name: Benadryl Ultratabs

economical.note: Target lists Benadryl Ultratabs Diphenhydramine Tablets, 100 count, at $14.89, which is $0.15 per 25 mg tablet.

health.note: DailyMed's Benadryl label states marked drowsiness may occur, a stronger warning than Zyrtec's "drowsiness may occur," and that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness. Diphenhydramine is an older, first-generation antihistamine, unlike cetirizine or loratadine.

accessibility.note: Benadryl is a nationally marketed brand product, not a single retailer's private label, unlike Target's up & up diphenhydramine.

products.description: The main diphenhydramine antihistamine brand; its label warns of marked drowsiness, stronger wording than the newer antihistamines carry.

products.name: up & up Diphenhydramine

economical.note: Target lists up & up Diphenhydramine HCl Allergy Relief Tablets, 100 count, at $3.59, which is $0.04 per 25 mg tablet, about a quarter of the Benadryl price.

health.note: up & up diphenhydramine is 25 mg diphenhydramine HCl, the same active ingredient and dose as Benadryl, and carries the same first-generation antihistamine marked-drowsiness warning under the FDA monograph.

accessibility.note: This is Target's up & up store label rather than a nationally licensed brand, so it can only be bought at Target stores or target.com.

products.description: Target's store-brand diphenhydramine, the same 25 mg dose and the same marked-drowsiness warning as Benadryl, at about a quarter of the price.

products.name: Claritin 24 Hour Non-Drowsy

economical.note: Target lists Claritin 24-Hour Non-Drowsy Allergy Relief Tablets, 30 count, at $19.99, which is $0.67 per 10 mg loratadine tablet, tied with Allegra and Zyrtec for the most expensive dose in this roster.

health.note: DailyMed's Claritin label states taking more than directed may cause drowsiness, implying the labeled dose itself is not expected to, and tells people with liver or kidney disease to ask a doctor because they may need a different dose.

accessibility.note: Claritin is a nationally marketed brand, not a single retailer's private label, unlike Target's up & up loratadine.

products.description: The main loratadine antihistamine brand, labeled non-drowsy at the directed dose, and, with Allegra and Zyrtec, the most expensive tablet in this roster.

products.name: up & up Loratadine

economical.note: Target lists up & up Loratadine Allergy Relief Tablets, 30 count, at $6.99, which is $0.23 per 10 mg tablet, about a third of the Claritin price.

health.note: up & up loratadine is 10 mg loratadine described on the product page as original prescription strength, the same active ingredient and dose as Claritin, which carries the same label warnings.

accessibility.note: The product page markets this as Target's own version rather than a name brand, and it is not stocked outside Target's stores and website.

products.description: Target's store-brand loratadine, the same 10 mg dose and warnings as Claritin, at about a third of the price.

products.name: Pepcid AC Maximum Strength

economical.note: Target lists Pepcid AC Maximum Strength Acid Reducer Tablets, 50 count, at $19.89, which is $0.40 per 20 mg famotidine tablet.

health.note: DailyMed's Pepcid AC Maximum Strength label carries no drowsiness warning, tells people with kidney disease to ask a doctor, limits use to 14 days without a doctor, and tells people with heartburn accompanied by lightheadedness, sweating, or dizziness, or with trouble swallowing or bloody or black stools, to seek medical care instead.

accessibility.note: Pepcid AC is a nationally marketed brand, not a single retailer's private label, unlike Target's up & up famotidine.

products.description: The main famotidine acid reducer brand; its label carries no drowsiness warning but limits use to 14 days without seeing a doctor.

products.name: up & up Famotidine

economical.note: Target lists up & up Famotidine 20mg Maximum Strength Acid Reducer Tablets, 50 count, at $4.79, which is $0.10 per tablet, about a quarter of the Pepcid AC price.

health.note: up & up famotidine is 20 mg famotidine USP, the same active ingredient and dose as Pepcid AC Maximum Strength, carrying the same label warnings on kidney disease, 14-day use limits, and alarm symptoms that need medical care.

accessibility.note: As a Target private label, this famotidine is not available at other chains the way Pepcid AC is; it is limited to Target stores and target.com.

products.description: Target's store-brand famotidine, the same 20 mg dose and warnings as Pepcid AC, at about a quarter of the price.

products.name: Aleve Caplets

economical.note: Target lists Aleve Pain Reliever & Fever Reducer Caplets, 90 count, at $11.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.13 per 220 mg naproxen sodium caplet. One caplet lasts 8 to 12 hours, so fewer doses a day are needed than with ibuprofen or acetaminophen.

health.note: Bayer HealthCare's Aleve Caplets label on DailyMed states this NSAID may cause severe stomach bleeding, with higher risk over age 60, with a history of ulcers or bleeding, on blood thinners or steroids, or with 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day, and that NSAIDs other than aspirin increase the risk of heart attack, heart failure, and stroke, which can be fatal. It caps adults at 3 caplets in 24 hours and tells people taking aspirin for heart attack or stroke to ask first, because naproxen may decrease that benefit of aspirin.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists Bayer HealthCare LLC, not a retailer, as the labeler of Aleve Caplets, so it is a national brand rather than one chain's private label, unlike Target's up & up naproxen.

products.description: The main naproxen sodium brand, one caplet lasting up to 12 hours, with the same NSAID stomach-bleeding and heart attack and stroke warnings as ibuprofen.

products.name: up & up Naproxen Sodium

economical.note: Target lists up & up Naproxen NSAID Sodium Tablets, 90 count, at $3.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.04 per 220 mg caplet, about a third of the Aleve price for the same dose. The product page says to compare it to the Aleve Caplets active ingredient.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's naproxen sodium lists 220 mg naproxen sodium per caplet, the same dose as Aleve, and carries the same stomach-bleeding warning and the same warning that NSAIDs other than aspirin increase the risk of heart attack, heart failure, and stroke, word for word as on the Aleve label.

accessibility.note: DailyMed names Target Corporation as the labeler of this naproxen sodium, so it is Target's own store brand, sold only in Target stores and on target.com, whereas Aleve's label is held by its manufacturer, Bayer.

products.description: Target's store-brand naproxen sodium, the same 220 mg dose and the same NSAID warnings as Aleve, at about a third of the price.

products.name: Bayer Genuine Aspirin

economical.note: Target lists Bayer Genuine Aspirin 325 mg Coated Tablets, 200 count, at $11.19 (prices vary by store), which is $0.06 per 325 mg tablet; adults take 1 or 2 tablets a dose.

health.note: Bayer HealthCare's Genuine Aspirin label on DailyMed carries the NSAID severe stomach-bleeding warning, an allergy alert, and a Reye's syndrome warning that children and teenagers who have or are recovering from chicken pox or flu-like symptoms should not use it, and says it is especially important not to use aspirin in the last 3 months of pregnancy unless a doctor directs it. It does not carry the heart attack and stroke warning, which applies to NSAIDs other than aspirin. Scored a little below ibuprofen and naproxen for the added Reye's and late-pregnancy warnings.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists Bayer HealthCare LLC, not a retailer, as the labeler of Bayer Genuine Aspirin, so it is a national brand rather than one chain's private label, unlike Target's up & up aspirin.

products.description: The best-known aspirin brand; its label carries stomach-bleeding, allergy, and Reye's syndrome warnings, and it is already cheap per dose, though the store version is far cheaper.

products.name: up & up Aspirin Regular Strength

economical.note: Target lists up & up Aspirin (NSAID) Regular Strength Coated Tablets, 500 count, at $4.29 (prices vary by store), which is under $0.01 per 325 mg tablet, about a seventh of the Bayer price and the cheapest dose in this roster. The product page says to compare it to the Bayer Genuine Aspirin active ingredient.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's Regular Strength Aspirin lists 325 mg aspirin per tablet, the same as Bayer Genuine Aspirin, with the same Reye's syndrome, allergy, and severe stomach-bleeding warnings.

accessibility.note: DailyMed names Target Corporation as the labeler of this Regular Strength Aspirin, so it is Target's own label, found only at Target and target.com rather than under a manufacturer's national brand like Bayer.

products.description: Target's store-brand 325 mg aspirin, the same dose and warnings as Bayer, at under a cent a tablet.

products.name: Allegra 24 Hour Allergy

economical.note: Target lists Allegra 24 Hour Allergy Relief Tablets, 30 count, at $19.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.67 per 180 mg fexofenadine tablet, tied with Claritin and Zyrtec for the most expensive dose in this roster.

health.note: Chattem's Allegra Allergy label on DailyMed carries no drowsiness or alcohol warning. It tells people with kidney disease to ask a doctor, since they may need a different dose, says not to take it with fruit juices or at the same time as aluminum or magnesium antacids, and tells adults 65 and older to ask a doctor. Scored level with loratadine, the other antihistamine whose label carries no drowsiness warning at the directed dose.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists Chattem, Inc., not a retailer, as the labeler of Allegra Allergy, so it is a national brand rather than one chain's private label, unlike Target's up & up fexofenadine.

products.description: The main fexofenadine antihistamine brand, labeled without a drowsiness warning, and tied for the most expensive tablet in this roster.

products.name: up & up Fexofenadine

economical.note: Target lists up & up Fexofenadine Hydrochloride Allergy Relief Tablets, 30 count, at $11.89 (prices vary by store), which is $0.40 per 180 mg tablet, about three fifths of the Allegra price.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's fexofenadine lists 180 mg fexofenadine HCl per tablet, the same as Allegra 24 Hour, with the same warnings: ask a doctor if you have kidney disease, and do not take with fruit juices or with aluminum or magnesium antacids. Like Allegra, it carries no drowsiness warning.

accessibility.note: DailyMed names Target Corporation as the labeler of this fexofenadine, making it a Target-only store brand; shoppers elsewhere need Allegra or another chain's own version.

products.description: Target's store-brand fexofenadine, the same 180 mg dose and warnings as Allegra, at about three fifths of the price.

products.name: Xyzal Allergy 24HR

economical.note: Target lists Xyzal Allergy Relief Tablets, 80 count, at $37.49 (prices vary by store), which is $0.47 per 5 mg levocetirizine tablet.

health.note: Chattem's Xyzal Allergy 24HR label on DailyMed says drowsiness may occur, to avoid alcoholic drinks, and to be careful driving. It also says not to use it at all if you have kidney disease, to ask a doctor first if you have ever had trouble urinating or emptying your bladder, and that it is not recommended while breast-feeding. Scored a little below cetirizine for those extra kidney and urinary warnings.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists Chattem, Inc., not a retailer, as the labeler of Xyzal Allergy 24HR, so it is a national brand rather than one chain's private label, unlike Target's up & up levocetirizine.

products.description: The levocetirizine antihistamine brand, a close relative of cetirizine, whose label warns of drowsiness and rules it out for people with kidney disease.

products.name: up & up Levocetirizine

economical.note: Target lists up & up Levocetirizine Tablets, 80 count, at $14.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.19 per 5 mg tablet, about two fifths of the Xyzal price.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's levocetirizine lists 5 mg levocetirizine dihydrochloride per tablet, the same as Xyzal, with the same warnings: do not use with kidney disease, ask a doctor if you have had trouble urinating, and drowsiness may occur, so avoid alcohol.

accessibility.note: DailyMed names Target Corporation as the labeler of this levocetirizine, so this up & up version is limited to Target stores and target.com, unlike Xyzal.

products.description: Target's store-brand levocetirizine, the same 5 mg dose and warnings as Xyzal, at about two fifths of the price.

products.name: Prilosec OTC

economical.note: Target lists Prilosec OTC Omeprazole 20mg Wildberry Tablets, 42 count, at $23.49 (prices vary by store), which is $0.56 per daily 20 mg tablet, or about $7.83 for one 14-day course.

health.note: Procter & Gamble's Prilosec OTC label on DailyMed carries a severe skin reaction allergy alert, says acid reducers may interact with certain prescription drugs, and limits use to one 14-day course, no more often than every 4 months, unless a doctor directs otherwise. It also lists symptoms, such as chest pain, vomiting blood, or black stools, that need a doctor instead. It is for frequent heartburn on 2 or more days a week, may take 1 to 4 days for full effect, and is for adults 18 and over. Scored below famotidine, whose label has no skin-reaction alert and a simpler 14-day limit.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists The Procter & Gamble Manufacturing Company, not a retailer, as the labeler of Prilosec OTC, so it is a national brand rather than one chain's private label, unlike Target's up & up omeprazole.

products.description: The main over-the-counter omeprazole brand, a once-a-day 14-day course for frequent heartburn, not for quick relief.

products.name: up & up Omeprazole

economical.note: Target lists up & up Omeprazole 20mg Acid Reducer Delayed Release Tablets, 42 count, at $9.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.24 per daily tablet, about $3.33 for a 14-day course and under half the Prilosec OTC price.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's omeprazole lists omeprazole 20 mg per tablet, the dose in Prilosec OTC, which its package panel says to compare it to, and carries a severe skin reaction allergy alert, says acid reducers may interact with certain prescription drugs, and limits use to one 14-day course, no more often than every 4 months, unless a doctor directs otherwise. it lists symptoms, such as chest pain, vomiting blood, or black stools, that need a doctor instead, as the Prilosec OTC label does.

accessibility.note: DailyMed names Target Corporation as the labeler of this omeprazole, so it is a Target-only private label; the Prilosec OTC label is held by its manufacturer instead.

products.description: Target's store-brand omeprazole, the same 20 mg daily dose and 14-day course as Prilosec OTC, at under half the price.

products.name: Nexium 24HR

economical.note: Target lists Nexium 24HR Delayed Release Capsules, 42 count, at $25.99 (prices vary by store), which is $0.62 per daily 20 mg esomeprazole capsule, or about $8.66 for one 14-day course.

health.note: Haleon's Nexium 24HR label on DailyMed carries a severe skin reaction allergy alert, says acid reducers may interact with certain prescription drugs, and limits use to one 14-day course, no more often than every 4 months, unless a doctor directs otherwise. It also lists symptoms, such as chest pain, vomiting blood, or black stools, that need a doctor instead. It is for frequent heartburn in adults 18 and over and may take 1 to 4 days for full effect, the same terms as the omeprazole labels.

accessibility.note: DailyMed lists Haleon US Holdings LLC, not a retailer, as the labeler of Nexium 24HR, so it is a national brand rather than one chain's private label, unlike Target's up & up esomeprazole.

products.description: The over-the-counter esomeprazole brand, a 14-day course for frequent heartburn with the same label warnings as omeprazole, at the highest price per day of the acid reducers here.

products.name: up & up Esomeprazole

economical.note: Target lists up & up Esomeprazole Acid Reducer Capsules, 42 count, at $15.29 (prices vary by store), which is $0.36 per daily capsule, about three fifths of the Nexium 24HR price. The product page says to compare it to the active ingredient of Nexium 24HR.

health.note: DailyMed's label for Target Corporation's esomeprazole lists esomeprazole 20 mg per delayed-release capsule, the dose in Nexium 24HR, and carries a severe skin reaction allergy alert, says acid reducers may interact with certain prescription drugs, and limits use to one 14-day course, no more often than every 4 months, unless a doctor directs otherwise. it lists symptoms, such as chest pain, vomiting blood, or black stools, that need a doctor instead, as the Nexium 24HR label does.

accessibility.note: DailyMed names Target Corporation as the labeler of this esomeprazole, so it is sold only at Target and target.com, while Nexium 24HR is a national brand.

products.description: Target's store-brand esomeprazole, the same 20 mg daily dose and warnings as Nexium 24HR, at about three fifths of the price.

products.name: Rest, fluids, and cold or heat (no medicine)

economical.note: No product to buy, so no per-dose cost.

health.note: Cleveland Clinic states a mild fever, under 101 F, usually does not need treatment with medication, and recommends fluids, rest, and a lukewarm bath instead. This applies to mild fever and minor aches specifically, not to allergy symptoms or heartburn, and it is not a substitute for medicine or a doctor's care when symptoms are higher or lasting.

accessibility.note: Requires no store, no delivery, and no money, only what is already available at home.

products.description: Rest, fluids, and a cool cloth or lukewarm bath, which Cleveland Clinic says is usually enough for a mild fever without any medicine at all.
